Take at the same times each day; with or without food

summary: Propylthiouracil is a thionamide antithyroid drug that blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and, at higher doses, inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3. Because of a boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal hepatotoxicity (including liver failure requiring transplant), it is generally a second-line agent reserved for patients intolerant of methimazole, for thyroid storm, and for the first trimester of pregnancy where methimazole's teratogenicity is a concern.
indications: Treatment of hyperthyroidism due to Graves disease in patients intolerant of methimazole and not candidates for radioactive iodine or surgery
Management of hyperthyroidism in the first trimester of pregnancy
Adjunctive management of thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm)

dosage.d: 300 mg/day in 3 divided doses every 8 hours
dosage.n: Severe disease/large goiter: 400 mg/day; rarely 600-900 mg/day
Titrate to thyroid function; once euthyroid
With beta-blocker, iodine, corticosteroid as part of regimen
Generally reserved when methimazole cannot be used

admin: Give in evenly divided doses, usually every 8 hours, at consistent times
Obtain baseline CBC and liver function tests before starting
Stop the drug and evaluate promptly for fever, sore throat, jaundice or dark urine
Effect on existing stored hormone is delayed - clinical response takes weeks
Reassess therapy if euthyroid state is not achieved or hepatotoxicity occurs
moa: Propylthiouracil inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking the iodination of tyrosine residues and the coupling of iodotyrosines, thereby reducing synthesis of T4 and T3. Unlike methimazole, PTU also inhibits peripheral type-1 deiodinase, decreasing conversion of T4 to the more active T3 - useful in thyroid storm. It does not inactivate already-formed thyroid hormone.

absolute: Severe hepatic injury attributed to the drug
relative: Bone marrow suppression / prior agranulocytosis on thionamides
Pregnancy beyond the first trimester (switch to methimazole)

preg: PTU is preferred over methimazole during the first trimester because methimazole is associated with congenital malformations; however PTU itself carries hepatotoxicity risk, so most clinicians switch to methimazole after the first trimester. Use the lowest effective dose and monitor fetal/maternal thyroid status.
lact: PTU is excreted into breast milk in small amounts and is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; use the lowest effective dose and monitor the infant's thyroid function.
renal: Limited data; use with caution and consider dose reduction in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: BOXED WARNING: PTU can cause severe, potentially fatal hepatotoxicity including acute liver failure requiring transplantation. Avoid in patients with hepatic disease, monitor liver function, and discontinue immediately if hepatic injury develops.

major: Warfarin / anticoagulants - antithyroid effect alters response; PTU may also have intrinsic anticoagulant activity (monitor INR)
moderate: Beta-blockers - clearance may change as patient becomes euthyroid (dose adjustment)
Digoxin - levels may rise as hyperthyroidism resolves
Theophylline - clearance changes with thyroid status
minor: Other bone-marrow-suppressive or hepatotoxic drugs - additive toxicity
interactions.food: May take with or without food; keep timing consistent.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol to avoid additional liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers free T4/T3 and may normalize/raise TSH; can prolong prothrombin time; may cause positive ANCA.

serious: Severe hepatotoxicity / acute liver failure (boxed warning)

monitoring: Baseline and periodic liver function tests; check promptly if hepatic symptoms appear
Baseline CBC; obtain CBC urgently with fever or sore throat (agranulocytosis)
TSH and free T4/T3 to guide titration
PT/INR if on anticoagulants or with bleeding signs
counsel: Stop the medicine and get medical help right away for yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, or right-upper-abdominal pain (liver injury)
Report fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers immediately - your white blood cells may be affected
It can take several weeks to feel the full benefit
Do not stop or change the dose without your doctor's advice
Avoid excess alcohol and tell your doctor if you are or may become pregnant
pk: Biochemical effect prompt, but clinical improvement over 2-3 weeks as stored hormone depletes
Plasma peak about 1 hour after an oral dose
Short, approximately 1-2 hours (intrathyroidal action outlasts plasma levels)
Short plasma half-life requires divided daily dosing (every 8 hours)
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light
pearls: BOXED WARNING - severe/fatal hepatotoxicity and liver failure: PTU is second-line behind methimazole except in thyroid storm and the first trimester of pregnancy
Unique among thionamides in blocking peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, making it useful in thyroid storm
Agranulocytosis can be abrupt - any fever/sore throat warrants an immediate CBC and drug hold
Switch to methimazole after the first trimester to limit hepatotoxicity risk
Associated with ANCA-positive vasculitis on prolonged therapy
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the regular schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, headache, fever, arthralgia, pancytopenia, agranulocytosis and hepatitis. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with CBC monitoring and treatment of marrow suppression and hepatic injury.
